I farm in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, so I will stay with the pattern I trust most: winter wheat followed by summer maize. At 63, I do not want to take on a crop that needs more marketing risk or more delicate field work. Wheat and maize fit my land, my labor, my machinery, and the local water conditions. I will keep most of my land in this two-crop rotation because it spreads income across the year and uses the growing season efficiently. I will use improved seed rather than traditional seed because I want steadier emergence, better lodging resistance, and more reliable yield, but I will avoid chasing overly fancy inputs. For wheat, I will fertilize enough to support tillering and grain filling, irrigate a few key times, and spray only when disease or aphids justify it. After wheat harvest, I will quickly rotary till and plant summer maize with a moderate fertilizer plan, fewer irrigations, and pest control mainly around early growth and late-season insects if pressure appears. I will manage costs tightly, keep tillage simple, and aim for stable output instead of maximum output.
